title: VM CPU Ready Contention on ESXi Hosts
exclusions: Reports an individual numeric vCPU instance whose native `vmware.vm.cpu.readiness` percentage is above 5% for at least three consecutive complete five-minute buckets, with local critical classification when the run peaks above 10%. Broadcom describes these as per-vCPU investigate/action bands; CPU Ready alone does not prove user-visible slowness or identify host saturation as the cause. The rule does not divide a summation by a hard-coded 20-second interval, use aggregate VM/host readiness as if it were per-vCPU, diagnose CPU limits/reservations/shares, co-stop, NUMA, over-sizing, host utilization, power policy, noisy neighbors, or application impact. Missing VM/vCPU metrics, changing vCPU topology, collection gaps, and stale dimensions are data-health findings. No VM resize, migration, resource-policy, host-power, or DRS action is performed and no compliance claim is made.
evidence: After deployment, retain vCenter/cluster/ESXi/VM/MOID/vCPU/workload ownership and resource-policy inventory; vSphere/vCenter and Splunk VMware Metrics add-on/DCN/DCS configuration and supported versions; enabled `cpu.average.readiness.percent` metric and dimensions; representative metric points; inventory/performance coverage, interval, delay, duplicate, dimension, and topology health; version-controlled `vmware_vcpu_ready_sustained` search, ACL, schedule, dispatches, and rows; vSphere advanced chart/esxtop plus application corroboration; exception/change disposition; and dated 5%/10% boundaries, three-bucket persistence, interruption, aggregate-instance exclusion, missing bucket, vCPU resize, late data, recovery, and routing tests. This documentation-only review collected no VMware metric, executed no SPL, and validated no production contention or application impact.

controlTest.positiveScenario: In an isolated metrics index and fixed completed 20-minute slice, write native `vmware.vm.cpu.readiness` points for `vcenter=vc01`, `moid=vm-101`, and numeric `instance=0` in three adjacent five-minute buckets with averages 5.1%, 6.0%, and 7.0%; expect one warning row with `consecutive_buckets=3`, peak 7, average 6.033, run bounds, and `use_case=UC-2.1.1`. Repeat at 10.0%, 10.1%, and 11.0%; expect critical because peak is strictly above 10.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Expect zero rows when all buckets are <=5%; exactly 5%; only one or two buckets exceed 5%; three breaches include a five-minute gap or an intervening <=5 bucket; instance is `_Total`, aggregate, blank, or nonnumeric; MOID/vCenter is blank; metric name/index is wrong; or points fall outside the window. Exactly 10% remains warning. Separate health must expose a missing expected VM/vCPU/bucket, DCN/DCS failure, collection-interval drift, duplicate series, stale inventory/dimension, vCPU topology change, and delayed metrics rather than treating silence as low contention.

dataSources: Primary data is the metric `vmware.vm.cpu.readiness` (`cpu.average.readiness.percent`) collected by Splunk Add-on for VMware Metrics through vCenter into the deployment's metrics index, shown here as `index=vmware-perf-metrics`. Required dimensions are stable `vcenter`, VM `moid`, and numeric per-vCPU `instance`; retain `host`, pool/cluster/ESXi placement and VM display name through qualified metrics dimensions or time-correct inventory enrichment. `_time` is required. Companion `vmware.vm.cpu.costop`, CPU utilization/demand/entitlement, VM limits/shares/reservations, host readiness/utilization, topology, and application telemetry support diagnosis.
app: Splunk Add-on for VMware Metrics (Splunkbase 5089) with its supported Data Collection Scheduler/Data Collection Node architecture collects vCenter metrics. A local observability app owns source-health and inventory reconciliation, the saved search, enrichment, fixtures, exceptions, dashboard, alerting, and runbook. Splunk Add-on for VMware ESXi Logs is not the performance-metric collector for this contract.
spl:
| mstats avg(vmware.vm.cpu.readiness) as ready_pct WHERE index=vmware-perf-metrics earliest=-25m@m latest=-5m@m BY vcenter moid host instance span=5m
| eval vcenter=lower(trim(vcenter)), vm_moid=lower(trim(moid)), vcpu=trim(instance), ready_pct=round(ready_pct,3)
| where len(vcenter)>0 AND len(vm_moid)>0 AND match(vcpu,"^\\d+$") AND isnotnull(ready_pct) AND ready_pct>5
| sort 0 vcenter vm_moid vcpu _time
| streamstats current=f window=1 last(_time) as previous_breach by vcenter vm_moid vcpu
| eval new_run=if(isnull(previous_breach) OR _time-previous_breach!=300,1,0)
| streamstats sum(new_run) as run_id by vcenter vm_moid vcpu
| eventstats count as consecutive_buckets min(_time) as run_start max(_time) as run_end avg(ready_pct) as run_avg_ready_pct max(ready_pct) as run_peak_ready_pct by vcenter vm_moid vcpu run_id
| where consecutive_buckets>=3
| sort 0 vcenter vm_moid vcpu -run_end
| dedup vcenter vm_moid vcpu
| eval severity=if(run_peak_ready_pct>10,"critical","warning"), warning_threshold_pct=5, critical_threshold_pct=10, persistence_minutes=15, run_start_utc=strftime(run_start,"%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ"), run_end_utc=strftime(run_end+300,"%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ"), use_case="UC-2.1.1"
| table vcenter vm_moid host vcpu severity run_avg_ready_pct run_peak_ready_pct consecutive_buckets run_start_utc run_end_utc warning_threshold_pct critical_threshold_pct persistence_minutes use_case
| sort 0 -run_peak_ready_pct vcenter vm_moid vcpu
description: Detects an individual VM vCPU that remains above Broadcom's 5% CPU Ready investigation band for at least three consecutive complete five-minute buckets. It uses Splunk's native readiness-percentage metric, labels a run critical only above 10%, and preserves VM/vCPU identity and run duration for workload and host-level correlation.
value: Sustained CPU Ready means a runnable vCPU waited for physical scheduling time and can contribute to application latency. A persistent per-vCPU signal helps virtualization and workload owners distinguish transient scheduling noise from conditions worth checking for host demand, VM over-sizing, limits, co-stop, placement, or resource policy—without assuming CPU Ready alone proves user impact.
implementation: Deploy and qualify Splunk Add-on for VMware Metrics with supported DCS/DCNs and a read-only vCenter account, enable host/VM performance plus inventory collection, and verify the native per-vCPU readiness-percent series and dimensions in the metrics index. Build independent VM/vCPU/interval coverage, save the delayed four-bucket search, test strict 5%/10% boundaries and three adjacent buckets, then enrich and route findings with current placement, resource policy, application SLO, and owner.
visualization: Lead with expected vCenter/DCN/VM/vCPU metric coverage, collection interval, indexing delay, duplicates, and stale inventory. Show per-vCPU Ready timecharts with 5% and 10% lines, a VM-by-vCPU heatmap, sustained-run table with MOID/name/current host/cluster/pool/resource settings, companion co-stop/utilization/entitlement and application latency, and placement/change overlays. Never merge VM aggregate, host aggregate, and per-vCPU percentages on one unlabeled series.
schema: Splunk VMware Metrics native per-vCPU readiness percentage with vCenter, VM MOID, instance, and five-minute time buckets
dataModelAcceleration: Not applicable. The source is a metrics index queried with `mstats`; no CIM data model supplies the native VMware per-vCPU readiness percentage and dimensions used by this detector.

knownFalsePositives:
A sustained per-vCPU Ready run is real, but Ready alone does not prove an incident or identify cause.

1. **Approved batch, backup, analytics, or load-test window** — genuine demand can raise Ready without violating the workload objective. Match exact VM/MOID, job/change, owner, bounded interval, expected SLO, and expiry; do not suppress every nightly period.

2. **CPU limit or resource-pool policy** — a VM can wait because of its own limit or parent pool rather than host physical exhaustion. Inspect limits, reservations, shares, entitlement and `%MLMTD`/equivalent before adding host capacity.

3. **Oversized multi-vCPU VM and co-stop** — too many vCPUs can increase scheduling difficulty. Review per-vCPU Ready, co-stop, usage/demand, NUMA topology and workload scaling; never remove vCPUs automatically.

4. **Short placement transition** — vMotion, DRS, host maintenance, power management, or restart can coincide with genuine transient scheduling delay. This rule requires 15 minutes; still correlate exact placement/change and current state.

5. **Metric instance or topology drift** — vCPU resize, MOID lifecycle, duplicate vCenter collection, aggregate instance, or stale inventory can misidentify series. Reconcile current VM/vCPU inventory and repair source health.

6. **Application unaffected** — Broadcom cautions that CPU Ready is one troubleshooting input. Correlate guest/application response, demand, co-stop, host utilization/latency and business SLO before declaring impact.

7. **Custom collection interval or rollup** — the native percentage avoids the old fixed-20-second divisor, but missing/irregular points and rollup still affect persistence. Display interval/coverage and test the deployed series.

Suppress notification only by exact vCenter/MOID/vCPU and condition with owner, reason, change, start, and finite expiry. Never suppress DCN/DCS, expected VM/vCPU/bucket, duplicate series, stale inventory, interval, or delay health.

detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites and corrected metric contract

Assign vCenter/ESXi, capacity/DRS, workload/application, Splunk VMware collection, Splunk content, and incident owners. Inventory each vCenter, cluster, host, VM MOID/name, current placement, numeric vCPU instances/count/topology, CPU limits/reservations/shares/resource pool, NUMA, criticality, workload SLO, maintenance and owner. Deploy a currently supported Splunk Add-on for VMware Metrics architecture with Data Collection Scheduler and sized Data Collection Nodes according to Splunk guidance. Use a vendor-documented read-only vCenter collection role qualified for the deployed add-on; the old invented `System.View` plus console-interact recipe is neither established here nor required by this search. This review ran no versions, so no `splunkVersions` claim is made.

Broadcom defines CPU Ready as time a VM/vCPU was ready but waiting to be scheduled. It documents under about 5% per vCPU as benign, 5–10% investigate, and above 10% noticeable/action territory, while warning that Ready must be interpreted with actual performance and related metrics. The add-on publishes native `cpu.average.readiness.percent` as `vmware.vm.cpu.readiness`. Use that percentage. The removed query divided a summation by 20,000, which is valid only for a 20-second interval; Broadcom's correct summation formula requires the actual sample interval.

## Step 1 — Configure and prove VMware metrics collection

Enable `hostvmperf` and VM/host inventory in the supported collection configuration and ensure `cpu.average.readiness.percent` is allowed. Confirm data lands in the chosen metrics index (the example uses `vmware-perf-metrics`) with `metric_name=vmware.vm.cpu.readiness` and stable `vcenter`, VM `moid`, numeric per-vCPU `instance`, `_time`, and qualified placement/name dimensions. Inspect actual metric dimensions from each supported add-on version; enrich from inventory by vCenter/MOID and event-time-valid placement rather than assuming `host` always means ESXi hostname.

Set/verify a five-minute performance interval if this detector uses five-minute buckets, and ensure vCenter statistics level/retention supplies the metric. Splunk documents collection-interval mismatch as a failure mode. Build independent health for DCS/DCN heartbeat/job errors, vCenter auth/TLS/API, expected vCenter/host/VM/vCPU series, numeric versus aggregate instance, missing five-minute bucket, interval drift, duplicate vCenter/DCN series, stale VM/placement inventory, MOID lifecycle, vCPU resize, future time, and indexing delay. Silence is unknown, not low Ready.

## Step 2 — Save and understand the mstats search

Save sidecar SPL as `vmware_vcpu_ready_sustained`. Run every 20 minutes over `earliest=-25m@m latest=-5m@m`, a completed 20-minute slice after five minutes of measured metric-index delay. Adjust delay and schedule together without gaps/overlap. `mstats` directly averages the readiness-percentage metric into five-minute buckets by vCenter/MOID/host/instance. The post-filter requires numeric vCPU instances and strict `>5`.

After sorting, the first `streamstats` finds the preceding breached bucket. A bucket starts a new run when no previous breach exists or timestamps differ by 300 seconds. The second `streamstats` assigns a run ID; `eventstats` calculates count, bounds, average and peak. At least three adjacent buckets means 15 minutes sustained. The latest qualifying run per vCPU is retained. Peak strictly >10 is critical; exactly 10 remains warning and exactly 5 does not breach. These are transparent interpretations of the documented bands, not workload SLOs.

## Step 3 — Validate percentage, identity, and persistence

Use an isolated metrics index with absolute times. Test 0, 4.999, 5.0, 5.001, 9.999, 10.0 and 10.001; one/two/three/four breached buckets; interruption and missing bucket; multiple vCPUs/VMs/vCenters; aggregate and nonnumeric instance; duplicate series; out-of-order/late points; old versus current MOID/name; vCPU resize; placement change; and exact dispatch boundaries. Assert average/peak, run interval, severity and idempotence.

In a nonproduction cluster or approved historical incident, compare the native Splunk metric with vSphere Client advanced performance charts and `esxtop` `%RDY` for the same per-vCPU entity and aligned interval. If only summation is available, prove `(ready_ms/(interval_seconds*1000))*100` with the actual interval and vCPU aggregation semantics in a separately reviewed search. Capture co-stop, usage/demand/entitlement, limits/shares/reservations/pool, host utilization/readiness, placement, NUMA, application latency and source health. Do not create production contention solely to test. Keep draft until owners approve metric/dimensions, inventory, fixtures, source health, timing, dashboard, routes, and response.

## Step 4 — Investigate before rightsizing or moving workloads

Alert text says `per-vCPU Ready sustained above 5%`, with vCenter, MOID/name, vCPU, current/time-correct host/cluster/pool, run average/peak/duration, metric interval/health, vCPU topology, limits/reservations/shares, co-stop, demand/utilization, application SLO, maintenance and owner. Responder sequence: verify metric identity/buckets and source health; confirm VM placement and resource policy at event time; compare sibling vCPUs and co-stop; inspect VM demand/usage/entitlement and host capacity/readiness/utilization; review NUMA and over-sizing; correlate DRS/vMotion/maintenance and noisy-neighbor demand; then confirm guest/application latency and business impact.

Never automatically remove/add vCPUs, change limits/reservations/shares, move a VM, enter host maintenance, change DRS/power policy, or add capacity from one result. Rightsizing can require guest reboot and application testing; migration can move contention; reservations affect admission/capacity. Use approved workload/vendor/change procedures with rollback.

## Step 5 — Troubleshoot and close

- **No metric:** verify DCS/DCN and vCenter configuration, `hostvmperf`, allow/deny lists, statistics level, metric index/RBAC, exact metric name, collection jobs and interval mismatch.
- **Only aggregate instance:** inspect collected dimensions/metric level and vCenter configuration. Do not apply per-vCPU thresholds to VM aggregate or host readiness.
- **Values differ from vSphere:** align VM/MOID/vCPU, timestamps/timezone, aggregation interval/rollup, percentage versus summation, and placement. Never reintroduce a fixed divisor.
- **Runs break unexpectedly:** inspect missing buckets, interval drift, late points and collection health; do not weaken persistence to mask gaps.
- **Ready high but host CPU low:** inspect VM/pool limits, entitlement, co-stop, NUMA, transient placement and power policy; host utilization alone is insufficient.
- **Ready high without app impact:** record workload/SLO evidence and tune routing with owners, while retaining capacity trend; Broadcom explicitly treats Ready as one troubleshooting tool.

Close after collection and inventory are healthy, per-vCPU identity and run math are verified, resource/placement and application impact are assessed, approved rightsizing/policy/placement/capacity work or risk acceptance is documented, and an owner-approved observation interval shows acceptable Ready and workload outcome.
grandmaExplanation: We watch each virtual processor to see how often it is ready to work but cannot get a turn on the real processor. We wait for the problem to persist and then check the virtual machine, its host, and the application before changing resources.
